# Publication hygiene

## Ask the index first

**Before making any decision, ALWAYS check if the index can answer first. Before searching with any tool (e.g., PowerShell, grep, sed, awk, etc), ALWAYS see if the index can answer first. Anything the index misses gets recorded as a miss and presented back to the user as a potential index improvement.**

Ask with `mise run graph:ask -- find <the problem in your own words>`, then read an entry with `mise run graph:ask -- read <ID>`. Report what it answered weakly with `mise run graph:ask -- misses --near`, and record a gap with `mise run graph:ask -- gap`.

The index answers from these, among others:

- `STD` entries of project lattice, standard
- `PRI` entries of project lattice, principle
- `PAT` entries of project lattice, pattern
- `MEC` entries of project lattice, mechanism
- `CAP` entries of project lattice, capability
- `TD` entries of project lattice, debt
- `PDD` entries of project lattice, pending-decision
- `BL` entries of project lattice, backlog
- `ADR` entries of project lattice, decision
- `TSD` entries of project lattice, discovery
- `TSDQ` entries of project lattice, discovery
- `LGQ` entries of project lattice, question

This skill's tasks span the activities documentation, licensing-and-ip, secrets-management and privacy-engineering, with the qualities confidentiality and privacy, and a task often needs several of them, named together and separated by commas. Read each row's flags and the line under it, where an entry's boundary, its successor and the debt against it are named.

This repository is public, and so is everything it publishes. Anything committed stays in its history, so the time to catch a problem is before the commit.

LATTICE's repository is public.

## Never publish

- names or details that identify a person or a client, beyond what the project itself names
- credentials, tokens, keys, private hostnames, internal URLs, mirror or index addresses, private repository paths
- notes true of one machine or one person's setup, such as local paths, installed versions, network behaviour or remotes. Keep them in that person's own configuration or agent memory
- text from a confidential source, quoted or close to it

## Sources and examples

- **Anonymise a real source** before it enters a sketch or an example. Replace organisations, people, places and reference numbers with neutral placeholders, and keep what the example needs to show.
- **Documents of a general-purpose layer stay domain-neutral.** Their examples come from several domains, and never cite a downstream project. Sketches and plans may name downstream projects.
- **Generated content drifts toward the domains a model has seen most.** Check AI-drafted examples for it, as the project's AI contribution policy asks.
- **Placeholder IRIs use `example.org`**, never a real organisation's domain.

Substrate and layer documents stay domain-neutral. See [GENAI_CONTRIBUTION.md](https://github.com/nebularis/lattice/blob/main/GENAI_CONTRIBUTION.md) §3 for AI-drafted examples.

## Delivery identifiers stay in working documents

How work was planned and delivered is not part of what a published document means. Production text never names it. Production text is everything under `ontology/` (READMEs, the documents generated from them, shapes, examples and the comments in them), the site's pages, and published ADRs outside their Provenance section (ADR-A127 decision 4, ADR-A126 decision 11).

- **Never in production text:** slice and phase identifiers (`ABC-1`, `XYZ-4.2`), question identifiers (`ABC-Q3`, `XYZ-Q2`), unit, epic and plan names used as labels (`ABC`, `XYZ`), technical debt and test row identifiers (`DEBT-49`, `ABC1-02`), and delivery phrasing such as "this slice", "the plan's brief", "flagged at", "at verification", "not yet written in ABC-2" or "open for the maintainer".
- **Say what instead.** State the fact the identifier stood for. A term not yet specified is "not yet specified". A rule decided in a published decision cites that decision. A modelling choice is stated as the choice, with its reason. A release note says what changed, never which slice changed it.
- **Production text cites only published decisions.** A citation of a decision that is not yet published waits until it is, or the text cites the published text that states the rule instead.
- **Working documents keep them.** Sketches, plans, status records, review requests, Validation Packs, the developer index, commit messages and agent memory use delivery identifiers freely, since that is what they are for.
- **Existing occurrences are debt, not precedent.** Some older documents and release notes still name slices. Do not copy them. Remove them when you next edit that text.
- **Check before handing off.** Search what you wrote in the production text for slice, question and debt identifiers and for the word "slice". Where a section is extracted into a generated file, the identifier is carried into it as well, so fix the source and regenerate.

Examples are `LG-1`, a phrase such as "not yet written in LG-2", `AIR-4.2`, `CCS-9b.3`, question identifiers `LG-Q3`, `P7-Q2`, labels `CCS` and `NRS`, and debt and test rows `TD-49` and `LG1-02`.

- **A migrated README cites only published decisions** (ADR-A127). The published-decisions check reports such a citation in a README not yet migrated and fails one in a README migrated to the ADR-A126 layout, which blocks a merge into `main`. On a branch a release note may cite the Proposed decision its change rests on, and before the merge the maintainer accepts that decision, or the note cites the published text that states the rule instead (PDD-16).

- **Check before handing off.** Search what you wrote under `ontology/` for slice, question and debt identifiers and for the word "slice". An extracted section carries the identifier into generated Turtle as well, so fix the README and regenerate.

## AI disclosure

If an AI agent is making commits, then the project's AI contribution policy, where it has one, governs the disclosure rules. In short:

- The trailer must survive a squash merge.
- AI-drafted text published under the project's name is reviewed by a person first, or labelled as AI-generated.

If a human is making the commit then disclosure is their responsibility.

[GENAI_CONTRIBUTION.md](https://github.com/nebularis/lattice/blob/main/GENAI_CONTRIBUTION.md) governs the disclosure rules.

- Substantial (tier A) and assisted (tier B) AI content is disclosed in every commit, with `Generated-by:` and `AI-Content: substantial | assisted` trailers, and in every pull request, with an "AI provenance" section. Review-only use (tier C) needs none.

## The deny-list check

Where a project has a deny-list check, `mise run check:deny-terms` checks text about to be committed against a personal list of terms, which is never published. It reads the first of these that exists, and passes when none does:

1. the file named by the variable the project sets
2. `${XDG_CONFIG_HOME:-~/.config}/<project>/deny-terms` on macOS and Linux
3. `%APPDATA%\<project>\deny-terms` on Windows

The file holds one case-insensitive regular expression per line, with `#` for comments. A line starting `!` names a path glob to skip, for a file where a term is legitimate. By default the check reads only the lines being committed (`git diff --cached`), and `--all` scans the tracked tree. A finding names the file, the line and the pattern's line number in the list, never the pattern.

It reads the first of these that exists, and passes when none does:

1. the file named by `LATTICE_DENY_TERMS`
2. `${XDG_CONFIG_HOME:-~/.config}/lattice/deny-terms` on macOS and Linux
3. `%APPDATA%\lattice\deny-terms` on Windows

It is one of the checks the commit hook runs, which `mise run bootstrap` installs (ADR-A133, skill `lattice-mise`).

## When something slipped through

Remove it in a new commit, and tell the maintainer. Rewriting published history is the maintainer's decision, never the agent's.

## The private overlay
A maintainer's private guidance lives outside every repository, at `~/.config/lattice/private/` (`%USERPROFILE%\.config\lattice\private\` on Windows), usually a link to a private checkout. `AGENTS.md` says when it applies. Its content is held to the same rule as the deny-list. It never appears in a repository, a commit or a pull request, in any form.
